overview: Manteño-Huancavilca is a broad archaeological label for coastal Ecuadorian societies, including communities of Manabí and the Santa Elena region. It should not flatten their distinct identities into one uniform empire. The map’s 1492 to 1500 slice and approximate coastal outline are coverage choices, not their beginning and ending. The Guancavilca identity maintained in Sacachún is more specific than this combined label.

periods.title: Coastal centers before European conquest
periods.summary: Manteño centers developed over centuries; institutional chronologies differ at their edges. Hojas-Jaboncillo preserves a major ceremonial and residential landscape within this longer history.

periods.title: Conquest and forced reorganization
periods.summary: Spanish campaigns and colonial resettlement changed coastal communities. Charapotó was devastated in 1534 and subsequently reconstituted as a reduction, a settlement organized under colonial rule.

periods.title: Communities and ancestral places
periods.summary: Sacachún’s collective territory and Guancavilca identity endured through changing colonial and national conditions. Its residents have actively defended their cultural heritage.

items.text: Manteño sailors used rafts fitted with sails for river and ocean travel. Spondylus shells were valuable exchange goods. These connections linked coastal production with wider trade, making seafaring skill an important part of regional influence.

The rafts could be steered with guaras, boards lowered or raised through the raft as adjustable keels. Marcos emphasizes this as a technical achievement: the sailors could choose a course rather than simply drift wherever the current carried them.

Power was not always held by men. Research on sixteenth-century coastal settlements identifies a woman ruling Achira and several subordinate lordships. The authors suggest that this center occupied an important position in regional trade, but emphasize that further documentation is needed.

U-shaped stone seats were associated with political and religious elites. Craftspeople carved them from single blocks of rock. Their striking form made a seat itself an emblem of authority: this was furniture with a public message.

At Hojas-Jaboncillo, the surviving landscape includes houses, temples, wells, water channels and storage structures. Managing water mattered alongside monumental building. The paths through the site pass evidence of everyday supply systems as well as ceremonial places.

A 2015 study of two domestic rubbish deposits at Loma del Secal identified bowls, cooking pots, griddles, ladles and spindle whorls. Broken household equipment gives archaeologists a much fuller picture than a collection of spectacular ornaments alone.

At the La Y complex, investigators recorded eight circular depressions thought to be underground storage structures. Their proposed function is useful evidence for food management, though a depression in the ground does not come with its original contents conveniently labeled.

Marcos interprets modified hillsides as productive landscapes with systems for collecting and distributing moisture from cloud forest. He links underground storage to surplus maize. This is the researcher’s reconstruction of how farming and political organization worked together.

Salango’s long coastal history can also be studied underwater. A survey recovered three diving weights, two net weights and an anchor. These finds illuminate marine harvesting, but the study’s multi-period setting does not assign every object specifically to Manteño times.

A clay figure in Madrid’s Museo de América wears a large headdress, ear ornaments, necklace and wristbands while seated on a stool. Although traditionally labeled a censer, the museum rejects that simple functional identification. Its elaborate appearance suggests elite ritual imagery; its original archaeological setting is poorly documented.

No securely translated preconquest sentence can be supplied from the evidence checked for this card. Gómez Rendón investigates old place-names and personal names to recover traces of coastal languages. Those linguistic clues and decorative images should not be turned into an invented alphabet or a made-up greeting.

Sacachún’s residents campaigned to bring home San Biritute, a stone human figure about 2.35 meters tall. Removed in 1952, it returned on 16 July 2011. Local associations with rain and fertility make its return a story of community memory, not merely the movement of a museum object.

At Hojas-Jaboncillo, the Catarama library includes a play and learning space for children. Community workshops also reproduce Manteño designs in screen printing. Archaeological knowledge can become something young people use and make, as well as something they see behind glass.

ending.text: Spanish conquest and colonial resettlement transformed coastal political life during the sixteenth century; Charapotó’s destruction in 1534 is one documented example. There was no single extinction date for all communities covered by this label. Guancavilca community identities and heritage claims continue, and the map endpoint of 1500 is earlier than these colonial changes.
